t: Count Unique Characters of All Substrings — Contribution Technique
o: We need the sum of countUniqueChars over every substring of s. A character contributes to a substring's count only if it appears exactly once in that substring, so instead of enumerating substrings we can flip the question: for each index i, in how many substrings does s[i] appear exactly once? For "ABC" every substring has all-unique letters, so the answer is just the sum of all substring lengths: 1+1+1+2+2+3 = 10. For "ABA", the two 'A's are unique only in substrings containing exactly one of them; 'B' is always unique, giving 8. With n up to 10^5 there can be ~5·10^9 substrings, so any approach that iterates over substrings (even O(n^2)) is too slow at the top end — we need an O(n) or O(n log n) method based on per-character contributions.
k: Flip the summation: count each character's contribution across all substrings rather than iterating over substrings.
s[i] is unique in a substring iff that substring contains no other occurrence of s[i]; its valid window extends from the previous occurrence of s[i] on the left to the next occurrence on the right.
If s[i] occurs at positions p < i < q (with sentinels -1 and n), it is unique in exactly (i - p) * (q - i) substrings.
Precomputing prev/next occurrence arrays turns this into a single linear pass.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force with Running Counts
a.i: For each starting index, extend the substring one character at a time while maintaining a frequency array of the current window. A character newly reaching count 1 adds +1 to the running unique count; a character going from 1 to 2 subtracts 1. This gives all substring answers in O(n^2) total time — fine for small inputs but too slow for n = 10^5.
s: For each start index i, reset a 26-size counter and unique = 0.
For each end j >= i, add s[j] to the counter; if its count becomes 1 increment unique, if it becomes 2 decrement unique.
Add unique to the answer after each extension.
a.t: O(26 · n²) worst case conceptually, but since the alphabet work is O(1) per step it is effectively O(n²) time — enumerating all n(n+1)/2 substrings once each.
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond the fixed 26-element counter (or O(26)).

a.i: Character s[i] contributes +1 to countUniqueChars(t) exactly when t contains s[i] and no other copy of it. If the previous occurrence of s[i] is at position p and the next at position q (using -1 and n as sentinels), then any valid substring must start in (p, i] and end in [i, q): there are (i - p)(q - i) such substrings. Summing this product over all i counts every (substring, unique-character) pair exactly once, giving the answer in linear time.
s: Build arrays prev[i] and next[i]: nearest index left/right of i holding the same character, or sentinel -1 / n.
Scan positions grouped by letter (or use last-seen map plus a second pass) to fill prev and next.
Answer = sum over i of (i - prev[i]) * (next[i] - i).
Use 64-bit accumulation internally, then cast/return as int (the problem guarantees it fits).
a.t: O(n) time — three linear passes to build prev/next and compute contributions.
a.sp: O(n) for the prev/next arrays (can be reduced to O(1) extra by tracking last-two occurrences per letter on the fly).

w: In an interview, mention the brute force briefly to show you understand the definition, then pivot to the contribution technique, which is the expected solution. Verify with "ABA": prev/next give contributions 2·1 + 3·1 + 1·2 = 7... careful — correct values are (0-(-1))(2-0)=2 for the first A, 1·3=3 for B, (2-0)(3-2)=2 for the second A, totaling 8. Common pitfalls: forgetting the -1/n sentinels, using 32-bit intermediates where products like 10^5 · 10^5 overflow before the final guaranteed-fit sum (use 64-bit in C++/Java), and double-counting pairs of equal characters. Edge cases: single-character string (answer 1), all identical characters (answer n), all distinct characters (answer n(n+1)/2). Follow-ups may ask for the O(1)-space variant tracking only the last two occurrences per letter, or generalization to counting substrings where every character is unique.
